source_text: Si ergo est naturale peccatum, non est voluntarium; si est voluntarium, non est ingenitum. Istae duae definitiones tam contrariae sibi sunt, quam contrarium est necessitas et voluntas, quarum confirmatio ex mutua negatione generatur. Nam sicut nihil est aliud voluntarium, quam non coactum; ita nihil est aliud coactum, quam non voluntarium. Simul ergo exstare, et velut vivere, duo ista non possunt; quia talis eorum natura est, ut tunc aliud vivat, cum aliud exstinguitur.
pass_a_gloss: If therefore there is a natural sin, it is not voluntary; if it is voluntary, it is not inborn. These two definitions are as contrary to each other as necessity and will are contrary, whose confirmation is generated from mutual negation. For as nothing else is voluntary than not coerced; so nothing else is coerced than not voluntary. These two therefore cannot exist together and as it were live; because such is their nature, that then one lives when the other is extinguished.

lemmas.lexica: LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself

pass_b_english: Therefore, if sin is natural, it is not voluntary; if it is voluntary, it is not inborn. These two definitions are as opposed to one another as necessity and will, whose affirmation arises from the denial of the other. Just as “voluntary” means nothing other than “not compelled,” so “compelled” means nothing other than “not voluntary.” These two therefore cannot exist, or as it were live, together. Their nature is such that one lives only when the other is extinguished.

choices.why: Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
